rules.statement: Model pure observation (a notification that cannot reject, mutate or return a value) as a published event, not as a mediator command; keep any seam that shapes the outcome as a mediator command.
rules.why: The type should tell a reader at a glance whether a seam can change the outcome, and a notification modelled as a void mediator command lets a throwing handler abort the operation.
rules.check: Look for new mediator commands with no result used only to notify (issued, revoked, rotated, succeeded) and for event handlers that need to reject, mutate or return something.

rules.statement: Publish an observation event as the last, side-effect-only step of an operation, after its outcome is decided.
rules.why: Observation must never alter the outcome of the operation it observes.
rules.check: Check that the publish call comes after the state change or result is decided, and that nothing after it depends on what the handlers did.

rules.statement: An event handler must not try to change the outcome of the operation that published the event; a handler that needs to is on the wrong seam and belongs in a mediator command or strategy.
rules.why: Events are side-effect-only observation, and a handler that changes outcomes breaks the guarantee that observers cannot affect responses.
rules.check: Look at event handlers that throw to block, mutate the event or shared state the publisher reads, or signal results back to the publisher.

rules.statement: When implementing fan-out to multiple observers, run each handler in its own try/catch and log a failure instead of letting it reach the caller or stop the other handlers.
rules.why: Per-handler fault isolation is the default, so a slow or failing sink never breaks the operation or the other sinks.
rules.check: Look for loops that await handlers or observers without a try/catch around each one, or that rethrow handler exceptions to the publisher.

rules.statement: Use the shared event publish/subscribe seam for observation, not .NET `event`, `IObservable` or ad-hoc observer collections.
rules.why: None of these isolate a failing subscriber, order by priority or resolve handlers from DI scopes, and ad-hoc collections each re-implement isolation, ordering and scoping.
rules.check: Look for new `event` members, `IObservable` usage or `IEnumerable<IXxxObserver>` loops added to report what happened.

rules.statement: A singleton that dispatches to scoped services must create a fresh DI scope per dispatch and resolve those services from it, never capturing scoped services.
rules.why: Capturing scoped services in a singleton leaks scope lifetimes; the publisher creates a scope per publish for this reason.
rules.check: Look for singletons that take scoped services in their constructor or cache handler instances, rather than resolving them from a scope created per call with `IServiceScopeFactory`.

rules.statement: Register event handlers with `TryAddEnumerable` (or the provided `AddEventHandler<TEvent, THandler>()` helper) so that several handlers can coexist without duplicates.
rules.why: The seam dispatches to every registered handler, so registration must add to the collection idempotently.
rules.check: Look for event handler registrations using `AddSingleton`/`AddScoped` or `TryAdd*` instead of `TryAddEnumerable` or the helper.

rules.statement: Define events as immutable records with typed properties, not dynamic metadata bags or dictionaries.
rules.why: Background handlers work from the event alone, and an untyped bag invites secrets.
rules.check: Look for event types with mutable setters, or with `Dictionary<string, object>` or similar bag properties.

rules.statement: Events and audit events must carry only identifiers, hashes and metadata, never tokens, secrets, authorization codes or key material.
rules.why: Events go to logs, audit stores and external buses, so a secret in an event leaks.
rules.check: Inspect new or changed event properties for token values, client secrets, codes, passwords or key bytes instead of their ids or hashes.

rules.statement: Derive everything an event needs before publishing it, and never read ambient request state such as `HttpContext`, `IHttpContextAccessor` or request-scoped services from an event handler.
rules.why: Handlers may run in the background after the request ends, so they must work from the event alone.
rules.check: Look for event handlers that use `IHttpContextAccessor`, `HttpContext` or request-scoped state, or for events whose envelope is filled in after publish.

rules.statement: Do not also log at a call site a milestone that the call site publishes as an event; logging, metrics and tracing of events are done by subscribing handlers.
rules.why: Logging, metrics and tracing are subscribers to the event, so logging the same milestone at the call site duplicates it.
rules.check: Look for `ILogger` calls right next to a `PublishAsync` (or audit recorder call) that log the same occurrence.

rules.statement: Don't report diagnostic logging of the exception behind an errored protocol response as a duplicate of the protocol-error audit event: the two are complementary.
rules.why: The ADR keeps operator diagnostics as ordinary `ILogger` calls (unexpected `server_error` at Error, other errors at Debug) beside the audit event.
rules.check: Before flagging duplicate logging, check whether the log is an exception diagnostic for operators and not a re-log of the published milestone.

rules.statement: Audit OAuth/OpenID Connect protocol error responses once per errored request from a single endpoint-level funnel, not by publishing an error event at each call site that produces an error.
rules.why: Errors reach the response through both thrown exceptions and returned error results, and publishing at each call site misses some paths and double-counts others.
rules.check: Look for endpoint or handler code that publishes or records a protocol-error audit event directly instead of relying on the endpoint filter.

rules.statement: A failure while recording an audit or observation event must be logged and swallowed so that it never changes the response.
rules.why: Observation must not alter outcomes, including a client's error response.
rules.check: Look for audit recorder or publish calls inside response paths that can throw into the response, without a catch that logs.

rules.statement: In a test project, assert that events were published by registering a recording event handler, not by mocking the publisher or inspecting logs.
rules.why: The ADR says tests assert events with a recording handler.
rules.check: Look for tests that verify events through publisher mocks or log output instead of a recording handler.

rules.statement: Publish an audit event through the typed audit recorder facade, which derives the envelope, rather than raw through the event publisher; publish a state-changing success at its call site.
rules.why: The recorder derives the audit envelope once, before publication.
rules.check: Look for `IAuditEvent` instances passed directly to `IEventPublisher.PublishAsync`.
